title: Fast and Accurate Probing of In-Training LLMs' Downstream Performances
claim: Conventional evaluation runs slow, costly generation and returns delayed feedback; a lightweight probe on representations gives near-instant feedback during training.
layout: 2 regions above and below a central training timeline; colored arrows loop to T_N+1
description: A title banner sits at the top. A horizontal blue arrow labeled 'LLM Training Process' runs across the middle, with circular checkpoint nodes T0, TN and TN+1. The top, orange-tinted region is labeled 'Current Paradigm'. An orange arrow leaves T0 into a 'Full-Scale Generative Evaluation' box that holds GPU cluster, database and document icons and the metric Pass@1(n). The arrow continues past a stopwatch showing 'Latency > 10 hours' and a coins icon showing 'Cost: High'. It ends at a red 'Delayed Feedback' warning box. The bottom, green and teal region is labeled 'Probe Monitor'. A green arrow carries LLM representations from T0 into a 'Single Full Evaluation' box and then 'Probe Training (lightweight)'. A teal arrow runs from TN through a single forward pass to the probe model icon. It reports 'Minute-level' latency and a green 'Instant Feedback' box, then returns up to TN+1. Orange versus green and teal color coding sets the two paradigms against each other.
caption: Workflow comparison between the current generative evaluation paradigm and the proposed probing evaluation paradigm for in-training downstream monitoring. Current paradigm suffers from high evaluation cost and excessive latency, resulting in delayed feedback to training progress. In contrast, probe can bypasses the generation process during the evaluation phase, thereby enabling rapid and timely assessment.
abstract: The paradigm of scaling Large Language Models (LLMs) in both parameter size and test time has pushed the boundaries of AI capabilities, but at the cost of making the traditional generative evaluation paradigm prohibitively expensive, therefore making the latency of LLM's in-training downstream performance evaluation unbearable. However, simple metrics like training loss (perplexity) are not always correlated with downstream performance, as sometimes their trends diverge from the actual task outcomes. This dilemma calls for a method that is computationally efficient and sufficiently accurate in measuring model capabilities. To address this challenge, we introduce a new in-training evaluation paradigm that uses a lightweight probe for monitoring downstream performance. The probes take the internal representations of LLM checkpoints (during training) as input and directly predict the checkpoint's performance on downstream tasks measured by success probability (i.e., pass@1). We design several probe architectures, validating their effectiveness using the OLMo3-7B's, OLMo3-32B's, and Apertus-8B's checkpoints across a diverse set of downstream tasks. The probes can accurately predict a checkpoint's performance (with avg. AUROC$>$0.75), have decent generalizability across checkpoints (earlier predicts later), and reduce the computation latency from $\sim$1 hr (using conventional generative evaluation method) to $\sim$3 min. In sum, this work presents a practical and scalable in-training downstream evaluation paradigm, enabling a more agile, informed, and efficient LLM development process.
